2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid First Drive: A Strong Case for Less SUV

The new hybrid Forester Wilderness begs you to ask yourself what your hobbies truly are.

Christian Seabaugh - Writer; Manufacturer - Photographer | Nov 18, 2026
See All 31 Photos

Sponsored by

With a wave of new rugged body-on-frame SUVs on the way and a slew of rugged crossovers like this 2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid already here, it’s time for off-road enthusiasts to have an honest conversation with themselves about the type of dirty driving they’re doing.

Off-road fans have long chosen Jeep-style body-on-frame trucks with low range, solid axles, and locking differentials. Those machines excel in the dirt but not on pavement, which suits people whose hobby is off-roading itself. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid targets buyers whose other hobbies simply lead them off-road.

The Best of Both Foresters

Subaru took the Forester Wilderness, which MotorTrend already rates as the most trail-capable in its class, and fixed its main flaw with the stronger, thriftier Forester Hybrid powertrain.

See All 31 Photos

A 162-hp 2.5-liter flat-four teams with a 118-hp motor in the CVT bellhousing and a 1.1-kWh battery under the cargo floor for 194 hp total. Subaru quoted no combined torque, though it should top the regular Wilderness’ 178 lb-ft.

EPA figures rise from 24/28/26 mpg to 33/29/31 mpg city/highway/combined, and the AWD stays full-time with a mechanical link between the axles.

Trail hardware matches the nonhybrid: a tuned suspension with 9.3 inches of clearance, X-Mode, 17-inch wheels on Yokohama Geolandar all-terrain tires, extra cladding, and unique fascias. Its 23.5/20.6/25.5-degree approach, breakover, and departure angles beat its rivals and most 4Runners.

Following owner feedback, Subaru also retuned the suspension for the hybrid’s added weight and a better ride.

See All 31 Photos

Revised AWD and traction control on every 2027 Forester spread power more smoothly on slippery ground, and hybrids in X-Mode now get more electric torque from rest for steep climbs.

The downsides: towing falls from 3,500 to 1,000 pounds, and there is no full-size spare.

The hybrid costs $1,000 more than the regular Wilderness, with prices from $41,970.

On- and Off-Road Driving

The pairing works as expected: the hybrid adds the low-end grunt the Wilderness lacked, and the Wilderness kit adds grip and trail comfort.

See All 31 Photos

On pavement it is competent if unexciting and quicker than the nonhybrid, with light steering and a suspension that absorbs potholes while keeping the body steady.

Most testing happened on dirt trails at a historic California rancho, where the crossover underpinnings gave a plush ride, even over rocks, mud, and squirrel holes at lower speeds.

See All 31 Photos

Tight dimensions, good sightlines, and ample clearance got it over obstacles. On offset moguls and 20-plus-degree climbs, the AWD and electric torque let it stop and restart confidently, rare for a CVT crossover.

See All 31 Photos

Complaints: X-Mode sits in a laggy touchscreen, drops out above about 20 mph, and forces hill descent control on, where a separate toggle would be better.

Let’s Be Honest

Hardcore rock crawlers should look elsewhere, but for reaching a fishing spot, a remote trailhead, or local forest roads, this Forester is right on target.
